newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan currency comments put pundits in quandary.
newsitem.headline: Japan currency comments put pundits in quandary.

text.p: A barrage of comments by Japanese leaders on exchange rates -- some of them seemingly contradictory -- has left market pundits perplexed and at odds over Tokyo's true intentions towards the downtrodden yen.
Ranged on one side are currency mavens who interpret recent remarks to mean Japan thinks the yen has fallen both too fast and too far, but doesn't know what to do about it.
Currency strategists in an opposing camp, however, say Japan still sees a weak yen as a plus for its sluggish economy and is just expressing distaste for the rapid pace of its fall.

"To the extent that people have conflicting views in their interpretation, it means they haven't been clear whether it's the level or just the pace (that worries them)," said Kenneth Landon, senior currency strategist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. Some analysts believe Tokyo is worried by the yen's drop below 115 to the dollar for a multitude of reasons, including corporate complaints that the weak yen renders their offshore investment meaningless and fears that the anaemic yen will trigger a collapse in Japanese share and bond prices.
Adherents to that view were jolted on Wednesday when Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said the Group of Seven (G7) nations agreed with the U.S. stance in favour of a strong dollar.
"The U.S. has been saying that it is seeking a strong dollar. My understanding is that the G7 nations share that stance," Mitsuzuka told a news conference.

Mitsuzuka's comment, which helped boost the dollar to a high of 119.20 yen in Europe later in the day, seemed somehow at odds with his own earlier statement on Tuesday when he dubbed the yen's slide "excessive" and said Tokyo would act appropriately to combat wild currency moves.

And only hours earlier on Wednesday, Bank of Japan Governor Yasuo Matsushita had hinted that the yen's steep slide might pose problems for the economy. "The pace of recent developments in the currency markets has been rather fast and we will continue to watch the effects on the economy closely," he said.

Some analysts said Mitsuzuka was merely reluctant to expose a currency conflict between Japan and other G7 members. Others said the finance minister, a conservative political heavyweight who took office last November, may have misspoken.
"He's not particularly knowledgeable," one economist said. "He's no (U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert) Rubin."
Rubin is a former executive of Wall Street investment banking firm Goldman Sachs.

Some also attributed official ambiguity to Tokyo's lack of a cure for the yen's rapid fall, given fundamentals which favour a stronger U.S. currency and Washington's persistent reiteration of its strong dollar stance.

"The Japanese government knows the limit of the power of intervention and...that intervention or the threat of intervention will only be temporarily effective," said Takashi Kiuchi, head of economist research at LTCB Research Institute. "Officials are waiting to see at what particular moment any particular action would have an effect," he added. "But they know the time has not come yet."

Analysts who believe Japan welcomes a weaker yen as relief for a fragile economic recovery that will have to swallow a bitter dose of tax increases this spring found little to trouble them in Mitsuzuka's latest words.
Such experts took Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto at his word when he said on Tuesday that he did not think the yen's fall had gone too far, but found wild currency swings "scary".

"I think what Japan is concerned about is the pace of the depreciation of the yen. They are concerned it might snowball and lead to a sell-off of Japanese assets by foreign investors," Deutsche Morgan Grenfell's Landon said.
"The Mitsuzuka statement is an indication of the fact that they really and truly don't want the yen to strengthen."
In the end, what Japanese authorities want may not matter much. The U.S. currency hit a fresh 47-month high of 119.40 yen in Tokyo on Thursday morning and sentiment remained bullish.
"What governments want with regard to exchange rates and what markets give them are of course two very different things," said one foreign economist.
